title: Good Code and Performance Analysis
oneLiner: What makes ML code good, and how to measure (not guess) where it is slow or memory-hungry.

what.html:
Good code is simple, modular, readable, fast enough and robust. To make it faster you first measure: time it properly (repeat many times) and profile it to find the one slow function or line worth fixing.

Everyday versionA good recipe has no repeated steps, is split into clear stages, is easy to read, doesn't waste time, and works even if the oven runs hot. If dinner is late, you time each stage to find the slow one rather than chopping faster at random.

why.html:
• ML code moves from notebooks to production, where others must read, test and fix it.
  • Copy-pasted preprocessing drifts apart and silently changes results.
  • Guessing at performance wastes effort; profiling shows where time really goes.

how.title: Rules vs learned rules
how.html: In traditional software you write if income > 50000: approve. In ML you call fit and the model learns the rule from data. So in ML, bugs are often fixed by changing data or features, not code, and the logic is harder to inspect.

how.title: Five features of good code
how.html: Simplicity (no repetition), modularity (small functions with clear inputs and outputs), readability (good names, style guide, docs), performance (time and memory), robustness (reproducible, clear errors, handles odd inputs).

how.title: Don't repeat yourself
how.html: If you clean three CSV files with the same five lines, write one function and call it three times. Copies drift: one forgets a step and nobody notices. Watch for repetition in preprocessing, feature engineering, training loops and prediction code.

how.title: Readable, checked code
how.html: Follow PEP 8: snake_case names, sensible line lengths, docstrings. Tools like pylint flag problems and give a score out of 10. training_data says far more than X.

how.title: Making Python faster
how.html: Pick a better algorithm, pick the right data structure, use NumPy/pandas instead of loops, overlap waiting for I/O, and run in parallel when needed.

how.title: Time it properly
how.html: One stopwatch reading (time.time()) is noisy, and the first run is slow from warm-up. timeit repeats the code and gives mean ± standard deviation, e.g. 1.812 ± 0.041 ms. Small spread = trustworthy.

how.title: Profile time and memory
how.html: cProfile shows which function takes the time; line_profiler shows which line. In a random-forest script, fit took about 63% of the time. memray or memory_profiler show which lines use the most memory.

demo.html: Increase the number of trees and watch fit dominate. Then parallelise it, or cache the data, and see the bottleneck shift. Optimise only what the profiler points at.

example.html:
A slow churn notebook. A team's nightly churn notebook takes 40 minutes. Profiling shows 70% of the time in one line that loops over rows to compute features; vectorising it with pandas cuts it to 2 minutes. The same feature code is copy-pasted in the serving API, so they move it into one features.py function used by both, run pylint, and fix the seed so results are reproducible.

Supplementary Amdahl's law: if a line takes 5% of runtime, even infinitely speeding it up saves only 5%.

misunderstandings: Good code is just the fastest code.
Readability, maintainability and robustness matter as much.
Copies drift; one function keeps logic consistent.
Repeat and report mean ± sd; discard warm-up.
I know which part is slow.
Profile: the bottleneck is often surprising.
takeaways: SE writes rules; ML learns them, so bugs often live in data and features.
Good code: simplicity, modularity, readability, performance, robustness.
DRY: one authoritative representation of each piece of logic.
timeit gives mean ± sd; time gives one noisy reading.
cProfile → which function; line_profiler → which line; memray/memory_profiler → memory.
thirty: In traditional software developers write rules, while in ML systems learn them, so logic sits in parameters and bugs are often fixed through data and features. Good code has five features: simplicity, especially not repeating yourself; modularity, with logical functions and clear inputs and outputs; readability, following PEP 8 with good names and docstrings and checked by pylint; performance; and robustness, meaning reproducible, graceful and well logged. To speed Python up, choose better algorithms and data structures, vectorise with NumPy and pandas, use asynchronous I/O and parallelise. Measure with timeit, which reports mean ± standard deviation over repeats, rather than a single time.time() reading. Then profile with cProfile for functions, line_profiler for lines, and memray or memory_profiler for memory.
